title: Proving Them Wrong
subtitle: A Life Beyond Fear, Epilepsy, and Other People’s Limits
author: Christos Solonos
blurb:
As a child, doctors said Christos would never live a normal life. Epilepsy, they warned, would keep him dependent forever.

He refused to accept that sentence.

Proving Them Wrong is the raw, powerful story of how he fought fear, manipulation, and other people’s limits — and built a life of freedom, purpose, and grit. From childhood defiance to university triumphs, solitude, and the courage to begin again at thirty-seven, Christos shares the real tools that helped him keep going.

This book is not guru talk. It is lived proof.

If someone has told you that you can’t — this is your reminder that you can. Grab a notebook, face the voices that held you back, and write the next chapter yourself.

chapters.title: Prologue
chapters.text:
"He'll never lead a normal life like other children."

The doctor looked at my family and delivered the rest of the sentence like a sentence:

"Chris will need caregivers beside him for the rest of his life, just to keep him safe from his epileptic seizures."

Something in me snapped.

NO!
I WON'T STAY INSIDE!
I WANT TO GO OUT AND PLAY!
I DON'T CARE WHAT YOU SAY.
I'LL SHOW YOU!

As a child, I was diagnosed with epilepsy. Hearing that I could never live a normal life made me furious. Who was he to decide what I could and could not do?

I would show him.

I would learn to ride a bike.
I would play football.
I would swim.
I would practice karate.

I would have friends.
I would grow up and live in my own house with my family.

That decision changed the course of that day, and the course of my life. I was determined to prove that epilepsy would not hold me back. I didn't care if the doctors said it was dangerous. I was going to learn how to live with it, and live like every other kid my age.

This book is the beginning of that story: how I chased my goals and built a good life against the expectations of family, friends, acquaintances, and almost everyone else.

I hope you find lessons here that help you do the same, to show them you are capable.

Because only you decide what holds you back.
And only you decide what pushes you forward.

chapters.title: The Diagnosis
chapters.text:
Growing up, I was a hyperactive kid, full of life, and hungry to learn martial arts.

Two things shaped that hunger. My godfather was a karate teacher. And every night I watched Dragon Ball Z. Together, they trained my mindset: find your limit, then push past it.

So that is what I started doing.

My first training ground was not a dojo. It was video games.

I fought as hard as I could to beat the toughest bosses. Day after day, I learned how to step inside a character's world so completely that my hands forgot they were holding a controller.

There was no controller.
It WAS ME in THAT WORLD.

That focus would serve me later, in sport, in school, in rebuilding a life other people said I could not have.

But even then, while I was learning to push, there was another force in the room.

A nagging voice.
Not only inside my head.
Around me.

chapters.title: The Programming
chapters.text:
Every day, while I focused on cartoons or games, a certain family member filled my head with “lessons.”

They were not lessons.
They were programming.

Women are sluts.
Never trust women; they only want your money.
Don't trust your “friends”; they only want to use you.
Why are you reading for so many hours? You won't learn anything new.

There were many more lines like that, designed to keep me quiet, controlled, and useful as her pawn.

That programming did shape how I built relationships as an adult. I am still working through it.

But it did not stop me from keeping an open mind.
It did not stop me from talking with people of all races and genders.

Someone tried to write my limits for me.
I refused to let that be the final draft.

chapters.title: The Vision Board
chapters.text:
When I was around fourteen, my father gave me an unusual assignment.

Get a piece of cardboard.
Cut out images and phrases from magazines that made me feel good.

At first it was slow. Then the words started showing up:

I'm happy.
I'm rich.
I have a lot of friends.

Then the pictures: me fit, at the gym, playing with kids, at the beach with a girlfriend.

When the collage was finished, I realized what I was looking at.
It was my life, from childhood into adulthood, laid out on cardboard.

I glued the vision board next to my bed. Every night before sleep, I imagined living the life on that board.

Over time, things began to move.
The biggest shift was leaving England for Cyprus.

That is where the vision board started becoming real.

I was finally free from the people, and the land, that had been my prison.

Cyprus became my sanctuary. High school years brought martial arts back into my body. Confidence rose. Limits showed themselves, then broke.

For the first time in a long time, I had friends.
Outdoor days.
A purpose.

chapters.title: Breaking Limits
chapters.text:
After high school, people told me I would not make it into university.
I was not smart enough, they said.

Guess what.
I got in.

My score was average, and I did not care. I was so excited I went to see the campus and checked every corner of it like I was claiming new land.

Student life took over in the best way: rope hanging, mountain climbing, cycling, drag racing, clubbing, living.

And still, the old voice found a new doorway.

Someone in the family told me not to talk to my cousin. She did not want him to “turn out like me.”

I asked her what that meant.
You don't want him to have friends?
To study?
To live a normal life?

Her answer boiled down to this: she did not want him gaming and becoming “nerdy.” She thought she had higher status.

Let me be clear about who she was dismissing.

A person who survived manipulation and child abuse.
Who lost a parent and kept moving.
Who moved country and rebuilt a life, with epilepsy trying to hold him down.

She did not want her son to become like me:
a fighter who never gives up.

Their image of me was that low. She said I would not pass my exams.

I hate to break it to her.

I passed with flying colours.

Those university years were some of the best of my life.

chapters.title: The Four Freedom Years
chapters.text:
What came next were the four best years I have lived so far.

Freedom days.
My own car.
My own house.
A girlfriend.

YEAH.
The kid everyone looked down on finally had what he wanted.

TAKE THAT, NAYSAYERS.

In those years I met people from everywhere. I made friends across different corners of life. For a while, it felt like I had a family of my own.

Then the old saying arrived on schedule:

All good things come to an end.

The relationship ended.
Friends moved on to build their own lives.
I was alone again in an empty house.

Everywhere I went, my eyes still saw them, like ghosts of a life that had already left the room. The pain got loud enough that staying put was no longer an option.

I had to get out.

chapters.title: Limassol & the Long Solitude
chapters.text:
So I left my city and moved to Limassol, where I still live now.

I arrived broke, in an old apartment with roaches, and an elderly neighbour whose shouting about prostitution kept me awake at night.

The happy life flattened into something heavy.
Depression moved in.

I had to get back up.

Over the next ten years I climbed: better jobs, more money, better apartments in places that actually had a social pulse.

Still, for long stretches I barely left the house, except for work, or the occasional event. Online, though, I stayed connected. People. Conversation. A world through a screen.

Then AI opened doors I did not expect.

In solitude I learned to draw.
I learned to build apps and programs, vibe coding my way into new skills.

That work changed how people saw me. They started trusting my eye. They brought projects for feedback and approval.

Even in the long indoor years, I was still building.
Still proving I could create a life, just through a different door.

chapters.title: Age 37: The Next Chapter
chapters.text:
These last two years, one question has been sitting with me:

What is the next step?

Working all day and coming home to a computer is not enough anymore. For five or six years I lived mostly in solitude, family sometimes, a few friends sometimes. Back in my twenties, during those four freedom years with Kazan and Prince, I went out more.

I need that again.
I need people.
I need a social life after the long solitude I built around myself.

I am thirty-seven now.
Yes, thirty-seven.

The number itself does not scare me. But if I want a family of my own one day, sooner matters more than later. I want to enjoy the fruit of the tree. More than that, I refuse to lose more years to fear.

For a long time I told myself epilepsy was why I did not want a family.
That was not the real burden.
I was holding myself back.

Until now, this has been my story.

From the next page on, the book changes.
Less about me.
More about you, and how you become who you want to become, not who others decide you should be.

I have proven my naysayers wrong many times. At thirty-seven I am not a guru and not a celebrity. I am a working example: a simple person who chose, as a child, not to give up because someone else said he could not.

You have that same power.
You can live your life the way you want to live it.

chapters.title: Who Do You Want to Prove Wrong?
chapters.text:
Enough about me.

Now we get to you.

Who do you want to prove wrong?
What is your story?

This part of the book belongs to one person only:
YOU.

Grab a notebook or a diary. You will need it.

Question 1
What is the heaviest thing from your past still holding you down?
What did they tell you that you cannot do?

Write every detail. Put it where you can see it.

Question 2
Who said it, and why?

Simple question. Heavy answer.
Who and why are often what you are still carrying. That is also what reminds you what you are fighting for.

Question 3
Write your pros and cons. Look at them carefully.

Some will be true.
Some will be a false image of yourself.
Use the real ones as fuel. Use the false ones as experiments, limits to test.

Question 4
What have you already proven them wrong about?

This one is for your power.
Proof that you can point to and say: I ACTUALLY DID THIS.

Question 5
What is holding you back RIGHT NOW, today, from the next thing on your list?

If you are still trapped with the naysayers, what stops you from moving?
A disability?
A voice talking you down?
Ask yourself the tough questions.

Question 6
What is your target, your real target?

Not the polite answer.
The real one.
The life you want when no one is watching.

Question 7
What is your current status?
Are you stable enough, at home, with time, with basic needs met, to give focused energy to your goal?

If chaos keeps interrupting, sort what you can sort first. Then protect time for the dream.

Take your time with these pages.
Honesty here becomes fuel later.

chapters.title: Deconstructing the Naysayers
chapters.text:
When someone tells you, “You can't do that,” it lands heavy.

Here is the truth:
People rarely project limits onto you because of who you are.
They do it because of who they are.

The three types of naysayers

The Fearful
They may care about you. They are terrified of failure. They want you safe more than they want you successful.

The Projectors
They tried and failed, or never tried. Your success would expose their excuses.

The Controllers
They prefer you weak. A confident person is harder to own.

Once you see their words as their issues, not your ceiling, the weight starts to drop.

The Filter Rule
Never take advice, or accept limits, from someone whose life you would not trade places with.

Ignore the noise: vague put-downs like “That's unrealistic” or “Who do you think you are?”
Keep the signal: real, useful advice from people who actually want you to win.

Don't argue. Outperform.
Debating naysayers wastes breath.
Don't tell them they are wrong.
Show them.
Let their doubt be fuel for the mornings you feel tired.

Action step
Look back at Questions 1 and 2 in your notebook.
Pick one negative line someone said to you.
Write why they really said it, fear, control, jealousy?
Cross it out with a thick black pen.

It is not your story anymore.

chapters.title: Routine & Energy
chapters.text:
You do not need twelve free hours a day to change your life.

You need one focused hour that belongs strictly to you.

If you work nine hours and come home emptied, trying to do everything at once is a fast road to burnout.

Two rules of energy

1. Know the difference between fatigue and fear.
Physical fatigue means your body needs rest. Take it. Recharge. No guilt.
Mental resistance is your brain making excuses because starting feels uncomfortable. Learn which voice is speaking.

2. Build the routine around your real life, not an ideal one.
Do not force a brutal 4:00 a.m. schedule if your brain wakes up at midnight.
Find the slot where your energy is highest.
Protect it.

Even thirty minutes of coding, writing, or learning compounds across a year.

Fix your environment
If your days are full of distraction, toxic people, or nonstop demands, your goals will always wait in line.
Audit the day: where does time leak?
Simplify: clear what does not serve your core target.

Action step
Return to Questions 5 and 7.
Name your biggest energy drain.
Pick one thirty to sixty minute window today that belongs only to your project.
Treat it like an appointment you refuse to miss.

chapters.title: The Experimenter's Mindset
chapters.text:
Stop waiting for the perfect plan.

Life is not a straight line.
It is an experiment.

Treat your goals like a video game level or a piece of code. Then failure stops being a disaster. It becomes data. You debug. You try again.

How to test your limits without breaking

Push past imagined boundaries.
Most limits are not real. They are mental walls built by fear, by old doctors' warnings, by habit.
Test them in small increments.
If you think you cannot handle something, do ten percent of it today. Watch what your mind and body actually do.

Know when to recharge.
Pushing hard does not mean running until you collapse.
Real strength is knowing the difference between breaking through a wall and driving yourself into the ground.
Test the edge.
Rest.
Get back on the horse.

Focus on the real target.
If a goal does not make you want to wake up, it may not be yours. It may be someone else's expectation wearing your name.

The trap: settling into a comfortable routine while the fire dies.
The fix: keep a personal project alive, coding, writing, creating, even when money is stable. Your brain needs something new to chase.

Action step
Return to Questions 3 and 6.
Write one limit you have assumed is true.
Design a mini-test for today.
Define your number-one target for the next six months in one clear sentence.

chapters.title: Your Circle & Your Proof
chapters.text:
You cannot build a strong future while surrounded by people who keep dragging you into your past.

Confidence is not only a feeling.
It is built on proof.

Find people with the same drive.
Spend time with people hungry for the same kind of forward motion.
When you are around people who push, it becomes easier to get off your ass and move.

Drop the dead weight.
If someone constantly brings negative energy, mocks your dreams, or pulls you down, you have a choice to make.
You do not owe your time to people who destroy your peace.
Replace toxic noise with cleaner fuel.

Build your proof stack.
When self-doubt arrives, your brain forgets what you can do. So keep receipts.
Do not lean only on hype or quotes.
Lean on your history.

Every obstacle you already beat, an exam, a health fight, a new skill, is proof you can do hard things again.

Action step
Return to Question 4.
Write three things you accomplished that people doubted.
Read them out loud when you feel stuck.
Audit your daily circle: who pushes you forward, and who drains you?
Spend more time with the pushers.
Less with the drainers.

chapters.title: Techniques From My Life
chapters.text:
I am not going to sell you polished guru tricks from YouTube.

These are tools I built from my own life, especially from living with epilepsy, and a couple of ideas I borrowed and made mine.

There are five parts.
Read one. Try it. Then come back for the next.

Part 1: Meditation

At first, when a seizure was coming, I shouted for help.

Meditation taught me another way: drop the spike of stress, breathe out, and observe instead of panic.

Over time I learned to sit back in my own mind and wait it out, count the seconds, talk myself through it, then return to the game, the day, the life.

Fear shrank.
Control grew.

Try this: once a day, sit still for two minutes. Breathe out longer than you breathe in. Notice one place in your body that feels tight, and let it soften.

Part 2: Limit Testing

Doctors warned me away from “heavy breathing.”

I asked what that really meant: running, cycling, football, exhaustion?

I tested carefully. Sometimes my hand showed the epilepsy signal. I paused, reset, continued.

My limit rose because I trained it in small steps, not because I pretended danger did not exist.

Push.
Read the signal.
Rest.
Raise the ceiling.

Try this: pick one limit you assume is fixed. Do ten percent more than usual today. Stop if your body warns you. Write what you learned.

Part 3: Awareness

Inspired in part by The Secret, and by the vision board my dad taught me, I practiced seeing myself from a second vantage point.

Present in the moment.
And also slightly behind myself, noticing sound, energy, and what my body was doing.

For me, that awareness helped me sense danger versus safety around seizures.

For you, it can help decisions: imagine the path if you act, and the path if you don't. Feel which future is yours.

Try this: before a hard choice, close your eyes and picture both outcomes for thirty seconds each. Notice which one leaves your chest lighter.

Part 4: Affirmations on Paper

I wrote goals and affirmations by hand and imagined living them while I wrote.

It kept confidence warm.
It kept the drive from going cold.

Not magic words.
A daily reminder of who you are becoming.

Try this: write three lines tonight in present tense. Example: I finish what I start. I protect my hour. I do not quit on myself. Read them out loud once.

Part 5: People as Fuel

The people around you are part of the technique.

If they push you down every day, they tax your progress, even if you are strong.

Sometimes the move is not another affirmation.
It is a hard choice: keep them, limit them, or replace them with people who share your direction.

In university I learned this in a simple experiment. Going out only to “meet girls” left us stuck and silent. Building a mixed friend group with shared energy made us more confident, and more alive.

Same rule for business, art, or any dream: find people with the fire you want. Borrow courage from the room.

Try this: list three people who drain you and three who push you forward. This week, give more time to the second list.

None of these tools require you to become me.

They require you to test what works for your body, your mind, and your life.

One part at a time is enough.

chapters.title: The Next Chapter Is Yours
chapters.text:
This book was never about me being a guru with all the answers.

It is about this:
no matter what label, diagnosis, or limit someone slapped on you, you hold the pen.

I did not prove my naysayers wrong by arguing.
I proved them wrong by showing up, testing my limits, and refusing to stay trapped in fear.

Now it is your turn.

Prove them wrong.
Show them who you are.

Final checklist
Never give up on your drive, even when life feels stable. Keep a fire for the next dream.
Filter the noise. People who quit their own dreams do not get to write yours.
Focus on your proof. On hard days, remember what you already survived.
Keep pushing forward. Time will pass either way. Spend it on a life you respect.

Your new starting line
You are standing at the edge of your next chapter.
Take a breath.
Look at what you wrote in your notebook.
Stop only wishing.
Step out.

Prove them wrong.

Final words
It does not matter who you are.
It does not matter what your life looks like.
It does not matter how long you have suffered.

All that matters is that you keep pushing forward.
All that matters is that you never give up.
All that matters is that you keep showing up.
All that matters is that you KNOW YOU ARE POWERFUL.

So get out there and show them what you are made of.

SHOW THEM.
THEY WERE WRONG.
HAVE A WONDERFUL LIFE.

Quick last note
If some of these strategies do not fit you, that is fine.
They worked for my life. Yours may need different tools.
Learn what works for YOU.

Stay safe.
Try what you like.
Do not be afraid to live.

We come here one time.
That is it.

If we live locked in a room with fear, what was the point?

LIVE YOUR LIFE THE WAY YOU WANT TO LIVE IT.

Have faith that something is looking out for you on the other side.

Something I always say:

If it is my day to die, then it is my day.
But if I can help it, I stare death in the face and say:

NOT TODAY.
